performers: Neal O’Doan, piano; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra; Peter Erős, conductor
intro: The first movement of Grieg’s only piano concerto opens with a timpani roll, after which the piano plays descending fortissimo chords. Neal O’Doan plays the whole movement, cadenza included, with the University of Washington Symphony conducted by Peter Erős.

sections.label: A · Flourish, then the first theme
sections.mNote: Timpani roll and piano cascade; the woodwinds then play the theme.

sections.label: B · Second theme, cellos, C major
sections.mNote: Second theme: a long melody in the cellos.

sections.label: A′ · First theme returns, piano, softly
sections.mNote: First theme in piano chords, then second theme in A major.

sections.label: Coda · New theme for oboes and bassoons

cues.title: Opening, timpani and piano
cues.text: A timpani roll begins pp and grows louder. The piano enters with fortissimo chords that descend from the top of the keyboard to the bottom, then rise in arpeggios to a chord held under a fermata. The Norwegian scholar Finn Benestad described these bars as Grieg’s calling card.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Piano Concerto Op. 16, opening bars (timpani roll marked pp; piano fortissimo cascade, then rising arpeggios, ending on a fermata), in the Schirmer two-piano edition edited by Percy Grainger (1920), p. 2: https://archive.org/details/concertoforpianoo00grie. Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon, “Edvard Grieg”: the opening piano cascades are “et griegsk visittkort”, a Grieg calling card: https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First theme, woodwinds then piano
cues.text: After a pause the orchestra begins softly. The woodwinds play the first theme, a march-like tune over syncopated strings, and the piano soon repeats it with arpeggios. Grieg drafted the concerto at Søllerød in Denmark in the summer of 1868.
cues.evidence: Jeremy Reynolds, Orlando Philharmonic programme note (2025): woodwinds introduce the first theme against syncopated strings; the piano repeats it with arpeggios: https://orlandophil.org/program-notes-opening-night-griegs-piano-concerto/. Composition at Søllerød from June 1868: Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon: https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme, cellos, C major
cues.text: The music modulates to C major, and the cellos play the second theme. On Liszt’s suggestion, the first edition of 1872 gave it to a solo trumpet. Grieg later returned it to the cellos, as he had first scored it.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass, Hollywood Bowl programme note: Liszt suggested a solo trumpet, it appeared so in the 1872 first edition, and Grieg later changed it to the cellos: https://www.hollywoodbowl.com/musicdb/pieces/2718/piano-concerto-in-a-minor-op-16. Henry T. Finck, Edvard Grieg (John Lane, 1906), p. 54: Grieg gave the second theme of the first movement to the cellos, Liszt suggested the trumpet, the score was published with Liszt’s changes, and Grieg later reverted to his first scoring: https://archive.org/details/edvardgrieg00fincgoog
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clara Schumann in Leipzig
cues.text: As a student in Leipzig, Grieg heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s Piano Concerto in A minor, which also opens with a flourish for the soloist. About fifty years later he wrote in his diary: “Every tempo stands indelibly stamped on my soul.”
cues.evidence: Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon, “Edvard Grieg”: Grieg’s diary entry on Clara Schumann’s performance of the Schumann concerto, written about fifty years later (“Hvert Tempo står uudslettelig præget i min Sjæl”, translated here): https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg. Laurie Shulman, New Jersey Symphony programme note (2019): like Schumann’s A-minor concerto, Grieg’s opens with a dramatic flourish for the soloist: https://www.njsymphony.org/assets/doc/NJSO-1920-Griegs-Piano-Concerto-online-extended-notes-9649b9559d.pdf

cues.title: Recapitulation in A minor
cues.text: The development fades and the first theme returns in A minor, played pp in chords by the piano. Later the second theme comes back in A major, a minor third below its first appearance in C major.
cues.evidence: Piano Concerto Op. 16, first movement, Schirmer two-piano edition edited by Percy Grainger (1920): p. 18, “Tempo Io”, solo piano in chords marked pp over horns and trombones; p. 23, the second theme in the orchestra at “Meno allegro”, now with three sharps in the key signature (A major), where p. 9 has it in C major: https://archive.org/details/concertoforpianoo00grie. The recapitulated second theme is in A major: Wikipedia, “Piano Concerto (Grieg)”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_(Grieg)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Liszt reads the manuscript, Rome, 1870
cues.text: In Rome in 1870 Franz Liszt sight-read the concerto from the manuscript, talking and nodding as he played. Handing it back, he told Grieg to carry on, that he had what it takes, and not to let them frighten him.
cues.evidence: Grieg’s letter to his parents about his second visit to Liszt, quoted in Henry T. Finck, Edvard Grieg (John Lane, 1906), pp. 36–37 (“Fahren Sie fort, ich sage Ihnen, Sie haben das Zeug dazu, und — lassen Sie sich nicht abschrecken!”, translated here): https://archive.org/details/edvardgrieg00fincgoog

cues.title: Cadenza
cues.text: The orchestra stops and the pianist plays a cadenza alone, in heroic style. At the première in Copenhagen on 3 April 1869 the soloist, Edmund Neupert, reported: “Already after the cadenza in the first movement the audience broke into a real storm.”
cues.evidence: Edmund Neupert to Grieg after the première, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon, “Edvard Grieg” (translated here): https://nbl.snl.no/Edvard_Grieg. Laurie Shulman, New Jersey Symphony programme note (2019): the cadenza “dazzles with romantic passagework in a heroic style”: https://www.njsymphony.org/assets/doc/NJSO-1920-Griegs-Piano-Concerto-online-extended-notes-9649b9559d.pdf. The cadenza (Adagio, then Presto) opens on p. 26 of the Grainger edition: https://archive.org/details/concertoforpianoo00grie
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: New melody in the coda
cues.text: The coda opens with a new melody, played by oboes and bassoons. The orchestra then drives the movement to its close.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, New Jersey Symphony programme note (2019): a completely new melody that oboes and bassoons introduce in the coda: https://www.njsymphony.org/assets/doc/NJSO-1920-Griegs-Piano-Concerto-online-extended-notes-9649b9559d.pdf. Grainger two-piano edition (1920), p. 32: “Poco più allegro”, the new tune cued for oboe: https://archive.org/details/concertoforpianoo00grie
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a Bergen merchant, who used Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party in concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. In his essay Min første Succes he recalled the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, but he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
